You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Grapes

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, grapes most commonly symbolize spiritual fruitfulness — the good fruit that God expects from his covenant people. Israel is repeatedly pictured as God's vine or vineyard planted to yield grapes, and the presence of good grapes (or their absence, 'wild/sour grapes') represents faithfulness or unfaithfulness, righteousness or its lack. In the New Testament this carries into the believer's fruit-bearing in union with Christ, the true vine.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 5:1-7 (the vineyard expected to yield good grapes but producing wild grapes; explicitly interpreted as Israel and Judah)",
    "John 15:1-8 (Christ the true vine; disciples as branches expected to bear fruit)",
    "Psalm 80:8-16 (Israel as a vine brought out of Egypt)",
    "Jeremiah 2:21 (Israel planted as a choice vine that became degenerate)",
    "Hosea 10:1 (Israel a luxuriant vine yielding fruit)",
    "Matthew 21:33-41 / Mark 12:1-9 / Luke 20:9-16 (parable of the tenants in the vineyard, owner seeking fruit)",
    "Micah 7:1 (lament that no cluster of grapes, i.e., no righteous person, is found)",
    "Matthew 7:16 ('Are grapes gathered from thornbushes?' — fruit as evidence of character)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Blessing, abundance, and prosperity of the promised land — grapes as a sign of God's material provision and the goodness of the land (and eschatological abundance).",
      "basis": [
        "Numbers 13:23-27 (the cluster of Eshcol carried back by the spies)",
        "Deuteronomy 8:7-8 (a land of vines)",
        "Genesis 49:11-12 (Judah's blessing of abundant vines and wine)",
        "Amos 9:13; Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10 (eschatological peace and plenty under vine and fig tree)"

      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ripeness for divine judgment — the 'grapes of wrath' motif, in which harvested and trodden grapes represent the wicked crushed in the winepress of God's wrath.",

        "Revelation 14:18-20 (the grapes of the earth gathered and thrown into the great winepress of God's wrath)",
        "Isaiah 63:1-6 (the divine warrior treading the winepress alone)",
        "Joel 3:13 (the harvest is ripe; the winepress is full)",
        "Deuteronomy 32:32 (grapes of Sodom, poisonous clusters)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Eucharistic/christological association — grapes as the source of wine and thus a symbol of Christ's blood and the cup of the new covenant; prominent in patristic exegesis, liturgy, and Christian art (e.g., the Eshcol cluster on the pole read typologically as Christ on the cross).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 26:27-29 ('fruit of the vine' at the Last Supper)",
        "John 15:1 combined with eucharistic readings",
        "Genesis 49:11 (washing garments in the blood of grapes, read christologically by church fathers)",
        "Numbers 13:23 as a patristic/medieval type of the crucified Christ"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The sour-grapes proverb — grapes standing for inherited guilt or its repudiation, teaching individual moral responsibility.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 18:2-4 ('The fathers have eaten sour grapes...')",
        "Jeremiah 31:29-30 (same proverb rejected under the new covenant)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "Grapes are genuinely multivalent in Scripture, but there is a recognizable consensus that the dominant symbolic frame is the vine/vineyard image of God's people and the fruit (grapes) God seeks from them, with fruitfulness vs. sour/wild grapes marking faithfulness vs. apostasy. The judgment/winepress motif and the blessing-of-the-land motif are well-established secondary strands, and the eucharistic association is strong in liturgical and patristic tradition though it technically attaches more to wine than to grapes per se. Confidence is 'medium' only because the term's meaning is context-dependent rather than singular; among biblical-studies reference works the fruitfulness reading is the most frequently listed primary sense."
}

Good grapes or the 'fruit of the vine' typically represent divine blessing, spiritual fruitfulness, and the blood of the New Covenant. Conversely, trampled grapes symbolize severe divine judgment, and sour or wild grapes signify apostasy and moral failure."

  "notes": "Grapes are rarely isolated from wine/vineyard imagery; Christian tradition strongly links them to the Eucharist via the Last Supper 'fruit of the vine,' while biblical texts equally support blessing, judgment, and corporate identity readings. No single meaning monopolizes published interpretation."

BOOK ENTRY
A nation's works ripened into its people — persons as the vineyard's yield: God looked for grapes — judgment and righteousness — and found men: Israel “like grapes in the wilderness,” the good man the missing cluster, the remnant the blessing left in it. Pressed, the grape gives blood — the cup of the covenant, or the cup of wrath, as the vintage is grapes or wild grapes.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 5:2 — And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
Isaiah 5:3 — And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard.
Isaiah 5:4 — What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?
Isaiah 5:5 — And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down:
Isaiah 5:6 — And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.
Isaiah 5:7 — For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

Micah 7:1 — Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.
Micah 7:2 — The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net.

Revelation 14:20 — And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
